title: Eat the fruit (Chagigah 15b)
hook: Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate, ate the fruit and threw away the peel
carry: eat the fruit, drop the peel

segments.voice: Yesterday, Acher, the teacher who left, and your line: he kept walking with him. Did you send that friendly word? Today, the same page, one step further. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

A pomegranate, split open. Red seeds packed tight, sweet and bright. Around them, a tough, bitter rind that nobody eats. Nobody throws away the fruit because of the peel, and nobody chews the peel because they like the fruit. The Talmud reaches for exactly this picture when it faces an uncomfortable question about Rabbi Meir and the teacher who left. Today, a fruit, a peel, and a surprising answer from heaven.
screen: `RED SEEDS, BITTER RIND.` → `AN UNCOMFORTABLE QUESTION.` → `AN ANSWER FROM HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Rabbi Meir walked behind Acher and kept learning. Tractate Chagigah doesn't let that pass quietly. It asks: how could he? There's a teaching, built on a verse in the prophet Malachi, that you should learn Torah from a teacher only if he is like a messenger of the Lord: someone whose life matches his words. Acher's didn't. The Talmud answers in layers. First: a beginner should be careful, but someone grown in learning can tell what to keep and what to leave. And then a story. A sage named Rabbah bar Shila met the prophet Elijah and asked what the Holy One was doing. Elijah said: repeating teachings in the name of all the sages, except Rabbi Meir. Why not Meir? Because he learned from Acher. And Rabbah bar Shila objected: but Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate. He ate the fruit inside and threw away the peel. And Elijah said: now God says, Meir my son says. In the story, even heaven changes how it speaks. The picture is generous, and it's demanding. Generous, because it lets a person keep what is true and good from a teacher, a parent, a book or a place that also carried harm. Demanding, because you have to actually tell seed from rind, and the Talmud's own caution still stands: this is for the one who knows the difference. Not every source is safe for every learner at every stage. But the one who knows the difference isn't told to throw away the whole fruit.
screen: `HOW COULD MEIR LEARN FROM HIM?` · `FOR ONE WHO KNOWS THE DIFFERENCE.` · `HE ATE THE FRUIT, THREW THE PEEL.` · `MEIR MY SON SAYS.` · then, large: `EAT THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to keep the good from a mixed source. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a source in your life that is mixed: a parent, a former teacher, an old workplace, a book you love that also has something ugly in it. Don't pretend it's all fruit. Name the peel to yourself, honestly. Then name one seed: one thing you learned there that is still good, still sweet, still yours. Hold the seed. Let the peel go, for now. When your mind argues, come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Eat the fruit. Rabbi Meir's way with the teacher who left: keep the fruit, throw away the peel, and know which is which. Today's word.
Your line: eat the fruit, drop the peel. Today, when you catch yourself rejecting a person or a book whole, look for one seed worth keeping. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Rabbi Meir's pomegranate is often cited in Jewish teaching when people discuss learning from mixed sources, along with the Talmud's caution that this takes maturity and discernment.

fork.setup: you're Rabbah bar Shila. Elijah tells you God won't repeat Rabbi Meir's teachings, because he learned from Acher. what do you say?
options: then Meir's teachings should be thrown out.

fork.reveal: he defends Meir with the pomegranate, and Elijah reports that God now says: Meir my son says.

original.note: Hebrew: pomegranate, the fruit in the Talmud's picture of Rabbi Meir and his teacher.

trapdoor: what you thought: eat the fruit is advice about healthy snacks.
what it means: keep the good from a mixed source and throw away the rest, as Rabbi Meir did with Acher.
what a scholar hears: Chagigah 15b: Elijah reports God won't cite Meir, until the pomegranate answer, and then: Meir my son says.

notes: The sage who meets Elijah is given as Rabbah bar Shila (Rabba bar Sheila); please confirm the name and spelling.

Elijah's report ('repeating teachings in the name of all the sages except Rabbi Meir' / 'Meir my son says') is paraphrased.
